Framewise displacement across days and runs

Benjamin Meyer

13 September 2026

This is the tSNR analysis repeated on head motion, with the echo factor removed: framewise displacement is estimated once per BOLD series, so there is one value per subject and run rather than one per echo. Two dependent variables are carried through in parallel, mean FD and max FD, both in mm.

Read the data

fd_results.csv is the long-format output of extract_fd.py: one row per subject and run, with the acquisition day taken from the ses- entity of the confounds filename.

fd <- read.csv("fd_results.csv") |>
  mutate(ID = factor(ID), run = as.integer(run), day = as.integer(day))

str(fd)
## 'data.frame':    128 obs. of  6 variables:
##  $ ID     : Factor w/ 23 levels "sub-10","sub-12",..: 1 1 1 1 1 1 2 2 2 2 ...
##  $ run    : int  1 2 3 4 5 6 1 2 3 4 ...
##  $ day    : int  1 2 2 2 2 3 1 2 2 2 ...
##  $ n_vols : int  325 333 333 333 333 325 325 333 333 333 ...
##  $ mean_FD: num  0.1089 0.0875 0.0947 0.0823 0.0967 ...
##  $ max_FD : num  0.981 0.796 0.983 1.313 0.726 ...
fd |>
  group_by(run, day) |>
  summarise(
    n_subjects  = dplyr::n(),
    n_vols      = paste0(min(n_vols), if (min(n_vols) != max(n_vols)) paste0("-", max(n_vols)) else ""),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Runs differ slightly in length — 325 volumes on Days 1 and 3, 333 on Day 2. Mean FD is an average and so unaffected; max FD is an extreme value and could in principle be biased upwards by a longer run, but the difference is 2.5% of the series and max FD is essentially uncorrelated with run length across the dataset (Spearman r = 0.038), so it is not a material confound.

Run-to-day mapping

Unchanged from the tSNR report (eeg_fmri_ext_SNR_1_v2.m:63, rest_day = [1 2 2 2 2 3]; runs 2-5 carry EEG):

Run Session EEG
1 ses-Day1_task-rest1 no
2 ses-Day2_task-rest2 yes
3 ses-Day2_task-rest3 yes
4 ses-Day2_task-rest4 yes
5 ses-Day2_task-rest5 yes
6 ses-Day3_task-rest6 no

The same two questions as before: across days (runs 1, 2, 6 — one run per day) and within Day 2 (runs 2-5 — the four EEG runs).

Choice of test

The tSNR report used a repeated-measures ANOVA, and that is kept here as the primary test so the two reports are comparable. FD, however, is a strictly positive, right-skewed quantity — max FD especially, since it is the largest of ~330 values — so the normality assumption needs checking rather than assuming. Each analysis below therefore reports, alongside the ANOVA:

  • Shapiro-Wilk on the paired differences, which is the assumption the repeated-measures ANOVA and paired t-tests actually rest on;
  • Friedman’s test with Kendall’s W, the rank-based equivalent of the one-way within-subject ANOVA (the “non-parametric test?” noted in instructions.md);
  • Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hocs next to the paired t-tests.

Where the two disagree, the non-parametric result is the one to trust.

# Prepare one analysis set: pick the runs, label the grouping factor, keep only
# subjects with a value in every cell (the design is fully within-subject).
prep_fd <- function(dat, dv, runs, labels) {
  out <- dat |>
    filter(run %in% runs) |>
    mutate(grp = factor(run, levels = runs, labels = labels),
           y   = .data[[dv]])
  complete <- out |>
    group_by(ID) |>
    filter(dplyr::n() == length(runs)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(ID = droplevels(ID))
  attr(complete, "n_all") <- n_distinct(out$ID)
  add_cells(complete)
}

# Every test for one analysis set.
fd_fit <- function(d) {
  wide <- d |>
    select(ID, grp, y) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = grp, values_from = y)
  ref  <- wide[[2]]
  diffs <- lapply(wide[-(1:2)], function(col) col - ref)
  shapiro <- data.frame(
    comparison = paste(names(wide)[-(1:2)], "-", names(wide)[2]),
    W          = sapply(diffs, function(x) unname(shapiro.test(x)$statistic)),
    p          = sapply(diffs, function(x) shapiro.test(x)$p.value),
    row.names  = NULL
  )

  list(
    aov      = anova_test(d, dv = y, wid = ID, within = grp),
    friedman = friedman_test(d, y ~ grp | ID),
    kendall  = friedman_effsize(d, y ~ grp | ID),
    t_ph     = pairwise_t_test(d, y ~ grp, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "holm"),
    w_ph     = pairwise_wilcox_test(d, y ~ grp, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "holm"),
    aov_log  = anova_test(mutate(d, y = log(y)), dv = y, wid = ID, within = grp),
    shapiro  = shapiro
  )
}

# Descriptives in the same shape as the tSNR summary tables.
fd_summary <- function(d) {
  d |>
    group_by(grp) |>
    summarise(
      n      = dplyr::n(),
      mean   = mean(y), sd = sd(y),
      median = median(y), IQR = IQR(y),
      min    = min(y), max = max(y),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(across(mean:max, ~ round(.x, 4)))
}

# Percent change relative to the first level.
fd_pct <- function(d) {
  d |>
    group_by(grp) |>
    summarise(mean = mean(y), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(`change vs first (%)` = round(100 * (mean - first(mean)) / first(mean), 2),
           mean = round(mean, 4))
}

# Caption noting how many comparisons were annotated.
brk_caption <- function(n_sub, pw, extra = "") {
  n_sig <- sum(pw$p.adj < 0.05)
  paste0(
    "n = ", n_sub, " subjects with complete data.", extra, "\n",
    "Brackets: Holm-corrected paired t-tests; unmarked = ns.\n",
    if (n_sig == 0) "No comparison was significant, so no bracket is drawn."
    else "*** p < .001    ** p < .01    * p < .05"
  )
}

day_labels <- c("Day 1", "Day 2", "Day 3")
d2_runs    <- 2:5
d2_labels  <- paste("Rest", d2_runs)

Part 1: across days (runs 1, 2, 6)

Summary of observed effects

Head motion does not differ between the three acquisition days. Mean FD is 0.107 mm (Day 1), 0.107 mm (Day 2) and 0.123 mm (Day 3). The ANOVA is nominally significant (F(2, 34) = 3.82, p = 0.032, ges = 0.042), but that result does not hold up: no post-hoc comparison survives Holm correction (smallest padj = 0.065), Friedman’s test on the same data gives p = 0.211 with Kendall’s W = 0.086 (small), and the effect drops to p = 0.065 on the log scale. The nominal effect is carried by Day 3 being about 15% higher than Day 1, not by the EEG day. Max FD shows nothing at all (F(1.24, 21) = 1.45, p = 0.249; Friedman p = 0.348).

Motion is also flat across the four EEG runs of Day 2. Mean FD declines slightly and monotonically after the first run — 0.102, 0.106, 0.099, 0.092 mm — but neither the ANOVA (F(1.78, 35.64) = 2.19, p = 0.132, ges = 0.025) nor Friedman’s test (p = 0.068) reaches significance, and no post-hoc survives correction. Max FD is equally null (p = 0.648; Friedman p = 0.319). There is no evidence of motion drift over the EEG session, and no evidence that subjects settle or deteriorate between runs.

In total, 0 of 36 post-hoc comparisons in this report survive Holm correction, which is why none of the four figures carries a significance bracket.

A caveat on max FD. The paired differences in max FD are strongly non-normal — Shapiro-Wilk p as low as 1.1e-05 — because the measure is the largest of ~330 values and is dominated by isolated events (one subject reaches 5.4 mm on Day 3, five times the group median). For max FD the Friedman and Wilcoxon results are therefore the primary ones, not the ANOVA. They agree with it here, so the conclusion is unaffected, but a future analysis with a real effect should not lean on the parametric test for this variable. Mean FD is much better behaved (Shapiro-Wilk p > 0.1 for the day differences).

Does motion explain the Day 2 tSNR loss?

This section is not part of the tSNR analysis being replicated; it is here because the FD result bears directly on how the tSNR result should be read. The tSNR report found a ~6% drop in grey-matter tSNR on Day 2, uniform across echoes. Motion is the obvious alternative explanation — a subject who moves more with a cap on would show lower tSNR for reasons having nothing to do with the cap’s effect on the signal.

The data above already argues against the simplest version of that: mean FD on Day 2 (0.107 mm) is essentially identical to Day 1 (0.107 mm), p = 0.956. A group-level tSNR drop cannot be produced by a group-level motion increase that did not happen. But that leaves a subtler possibility open: motion might still explain which subjects lost the most tSNR. Testing that needs the two tables joined.

tsnr_wide <- read.csv("tSNR_results.txt", na.strings = c("NA", "NaN", ""))
names(tsnr_wide)[1] <- "ID"

# tSNR averaged over the four echoes, for runs 1 and 2.
tsnr_delta <- tsnr_wide |>
  transmute(
    ID     = ID,
    tsnr_1 = rowMeans(across(c(r1e1, r1e2, r1e3, r1e4))),
    tsnr_2 = rowMeans(across(c(r2e1, r2e2, r2e3, r2e4)))
  ) |>
  mutate(d_tsnr = tsnr_2 - tsnr_1)

fd_delta <- fd |>
  filter(run %in% c(1, 2)) |>
  select(ID, run, mean_FD) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = run, values_from = mean_FD, names_prefix = "fd_") |>
  mutate(d_fd = fd_2 - fd_1)

joined <- inner_join(tsnr_delta, fd_delta, by = "ID") |>
  filter(!is.na(d_tsnr), !is.na(d_fd))

cat("Subjects with both measures on runs 1 and 2: ", nrow(joined), "\n", sep = "")
## Subjects with both measures on runs 1 and 2: 20

The change in motion and the change in tSNR are related across subjects:

cor.test(joined$d_fd, joined$d_tsnr, method = "spearman")
## 
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
## 
## data:  joined$d_fd and joined$d_tsnr
## S = 1874, p-value = 0.07453
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##        rho 
## -0.4090226

So motion is not irrelevant. The question is whether it accounts for the mean drop or only for the spread around it. Regressing the tSNR change on the motion change separates the two: the slope is the motion contribution, and the intercept is the tSNR change expected for a subject whose motion did not change at all.

fit_conf <- lm(d_tsnr ~ d_fd, data = joined)
summary(fit_conf)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = d_tsnr ~ d_fd, data = joined)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -7.2984 -2.1767 -0.7104  2.9830  7.5159 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)   
## (Intercept)  -3.7301     0.9524  -3.917  0.00101 **
## d_fd        -74.0616    34.7941  -2.129  0.04736 * 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 4.253 on 18 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.2011, Adjusted R-squared:  0.1567 
## F-statistic: 4.531 on 1 and 18 DF,  p-value: 0.04736
ggplot(joined, aes(x = d_fd, y = d_tsnr)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = "black",
              linewidth = 0.5, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "black", colour = "white", size = 2.6, stroke = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title    = "Change in motion vs change in tSNR, Day 1 to Day 2",
    subtitle = "Each dot is one subject; tSNR averaged over the four echoes",
    x        = "Change in mean FD (mm)",
    y        = "Change in tSNR"
  )

Both things are true, and they answer different questions. Across the 20 subjects with both measures, motion change does predict tSNR change, in the expected direction and with a respectable effect size: Spearman rho = -0.41 (p = 0.075), and in the regression the slope is significant (b = -74.1 tSNR units per mm of FD, p = 0.047, R² = 0.2). Subjects who moved more on Day 2 did lose more tSNR. Motion is a genuine contributor to the subject-to-subject spread in the Day 2 loss.

It is not, however, the cause of the loss itself. The regression intercept — the expected tSNR change for a subject whose motion was identical on the two days — is -3.73 (p = 0.0010), against a raw mean change of -3.84. In other words, essentially the entire mean drop remains at zero motion change. That is the expected result given the group-level numbers: only 10 of 20 subjects moved more on Day 2 at all, and mean FD across the group was flat, so motion has no mean shift available to transmit to tSNR.

The reading in the tSNR report therefore stands, with one refinement. The Day 2 tSNR loss is a property of the EEG hardware being in the bore rather than of subjects behaving differently while wearing it — but motion still modulates how large that loss is for a given subject, and a study using per-subject Day 2 tSNR as a covariate would do well to include mean FD alongside it. Two caveats on this section specifically: n = 20 is small for a correlation, so the slope estimate is imprecise; and FD and tSNR are not independent measurements, since motion enters the tSNR denominator directly through the temporal standard deviation.
